source_text:
παρουσίᾳ τοῦ σωτῆρος. Πάντες εἶπεν διὰ τὴν ἀπόφασιν καὶ τὸ ἐνδεχόμενον, ἐπεὶ οὐ
πάντες ἀπέθανον οἷος Ἐνὼχ καὶ Ἡλίας· εὑρεθήσονται δέ τινες καὶ ἐν τῇ παρουσίᾳ
ζῶντες. ἐν τῷ Ἀδὰμ δὲ λέγει ἀντὶ τοῦ διὰ τὸν Ἀδάμ, ὥσπερ καὶ ἐν Χριστῷ διὰ τὸν
Χριστόν. ἐν τῷ Ἀδὰμ οὖν ἀποθνῄσκομεν, δηλονότι κατὰ τὸ σῶμα, καὶ ἐν τῷ Χριστῷ
ζωοποιηθήσονται, δηλονότι κατὰ τὸ σῶμα· εἰ γὰρ πρὸ Χριστοῦ αἱ ψυχαὶ ζῶσιν, καὶ
μετὰ Χριστὸν αὗται μόναι πάλιν ζῶσιν, τί τὸ περισσὸν τῆς οἰκονομίας; 1 Kor 15,23–
25 Τάγμα λέγει δικαίων καὶ ἀδίκων, οὐκ ἰδικῶς δὲ τοὺς τοῦ Χριστοῦ ὧδε τοὺς
πιστοὺς λέγει ἀλλὰ πάντας, ὅτι πάντες εἰσὶ Χριστοῦ. ἐν δὲ τῇ παρουσίᾳ αὐτοῦ ἔσται
πάντων ἡ ἀνάστασις, ὅτε καὶ τὸ τέλος, τὸ καταβαπτισθῆναι καὶ τὸν θάνατον καὶ τὸν
διάβολον· τοῦτο γὰρ τοῦ κόσμου τὸ τέλος. Τὴν βασιλείαν λέγει οὐ τὴν ἑαυτοῦ, ἀλλ'
ἣν ἥρπασεν ὁ πονηρὸς καταβαλὼν τὸν Ἀδὰμ καὶ τοὺς ἀπ' αὐτοῦ. ταύτην δὲ
παραδιδοὺς τῷ πατρὶ οὐκ ἀλλότριος αὐτῆς ἔσται· συμβασιλεύει γὰρ ὁ υἱὸς τῷ πατρί.
οὐ προθεσμίας δέ ἐστι δηλωτικὸν τὸ ἄρχειν ἀλλ' ἐπιτάσεως, ὥσπερ εἴ τις λέγει· δεῖ
με ἐναρετῶς ζῆν ἕως ἂν κατορθώσω δικαιοσύνην. οὐ γὰρ τοῦτο λέγει ὅτι
κατορθώσας οὐκέτι ζήσομαι ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ, ἀλλ' ὅτι τὴν δικαιοσύνην δι' ἐναρέτου
μοι σπουδῆς κατορθωτέον. καὶ ἐν προφήταις δὲ τὸ ἕως οὐ πάντως προθεσμίας ἐστὶν
ἀλλ' ἐπιστάσεως, ὡς καὶ ἐν παλαιᾷ ἔνθα φησίν· ἐγώ εἰμι ἐγώ, εἰμὶ ἕως ἂν
καταγηράσητε. οὐ γὰρ ὅρον τοῦ εἶναι αὐτὸν τὸ γῆρας τῶν γηρόντων λέγει, ἀλλ' ὅτι
κἂν ὑμεῖς γηράσητε, ἐγὼ εἰμί, οὐ συγγήρων ὑμῖν ἀλλ' ἀεὶ ὤν. οὕτω καὶ νῦν τὸ ἄχρις
οὗ πέρας σημαίνει. ὃ δὲ λέγει τοῦτό ἐστιν· οὐ διακοπήσεται αὐτοῦ μεταξὺ ἡ βασιλεία
οὐδ' ἐπιλήψουσιν οἱ πιστεύοντες ἕως ἂν κατορθωθῇ ἃ προέθετο, καὶ κατορθώσας
καὶ βασιλεύσει διηνεκῶς. 275 1 Kor 15,29 Εἰ τὰ σώματα, φησί, νεκρὰ μένει καὶ οὐκ
ἀνίσταται, τί ὑπὲρ τούτων τῶν νεκρῶν ὡς ἀνισταμένων καὶ κριθησομένων
βαπτιζόμεθα, ἄφεσιν λαμβάνοντες ἁμαρτημάτων ὑπὲρ τοῦ μὴ κριθῆναι; 1 Kor 15,32
Ὅσον, φησίν, ἐπ' ἀνθρώπῳ ἐθηριομάχησα, ὁ δὲ θεὸς ἔσωσέν με. 1 Kor 15,35–38 Οἱ
Ἕλληνες ἀντιλέγουσιν ὅτι σπέρμα διχασθὲν οὐκέτι βλαστάνει. ἄρα οὖν καὶ
ἄνθρωπος ἀποκοπεὶς τὸν πόδα ἢ ὄλως ἀκρωτηριασθεὶς τὸ σῶμα οὐκέτι ἐγείρεται.
ἀγνοοῦντες ὅτι οὐ φύσις φύσει παρετέθη, ἀλλ' ἡ δύναμις τοῦ πεποιηκότος, τοῦτ' ἔστι
τοῦ σπέρματος τὴν βλαστητικὴν φύσιν καὶ τὴν σπερματικὴν δύναμιν τίς ἔδωκεν;
οὐχ ὁ θεός; τίς ὁ ποιῶν ἀποθανεῖν πρῶτον τὸν σπόρον, εἶτα ἀνίστασθαι; οὐχ ὁ θεός;
pass_a_gloss: [15:21-22 note, continued] ...coming of the Savior. [Second form] [Not printed again: He said 'all' because of the sentence and the possible, since not all died, such as Enoch and Elijah; and some will be found living also at the coming.] And he says 'in Adam' instead of 'because of Adam', as also 'in Christ' because of Christ. So in Adam we die, clearly according to the body, and in Christ they will be made alive, clearly according to the body; for if before Christ the souls live, and after Christ these alone live again, what is the extra of the plan? [Label 1 Kor 15,23-25] He says order of righteous and unrighteous, and here he does not mean specifically by 'those of Christ' the faithful, but all, because all are Christ's. And at his coming will be the resurrection of all, when also the end, the being plunged under of both death and the devil; for this is the end of the world. He says the kingdom not his own, but the one which the evil one seized, having thrown down Adam and those from him. And handing this over to the Father he will not be a stranger to it; for the Son reigns together with the Father. And the reigning is not indicative of a time limit but of intensification, as if someone says: I must live virtuously until I achieve righteousness. For he does not say this, that having achieved it I will no longer live in righteousness, but that righteousness must be achieved by me through virtuous eagerness. And in prophets too the 'until' is not altogether of a time limit but of emphasis, as also in the old [Scripture] where he says: 'I am I, I am until you grow old.' For he does not say the old age of those growing old is a boundary of his being, but that even if you grow old, I am, not growing old with you but always being. So also now the 'until' signifies an end [goal]. And what he says is this: his kingdom will not be cut off in between, nor will those believing fail (Greek ἐπιλήψουσιν, read ἐπιλείψουσιν), until the things he purposed are achieved, and having achieved [them] he will also reign continually. [Page 275; label 1 Kor 15,29] If the bodies, he says, remain dead and do not rise, why are we baptized for these dead as rising and going to be judged, receiving forgiveness of sins for the sake of not being judged? [Label 1 Kor 15,32] As far as [depended] on man, he says, I fought beasts, but God saved me. [Label 1 Kor 15,35-38] The Greeks object that a seed divided no longer sprouts. So then also a man having had his foot cut off or altogether mutilated in body is no longer raised; not knowing that not nature was set beside nature, but the power of the one who made [it]; that is, who gave the sprouting nature of the seed and the seminal power? Not God? Who is the one making the seed first die, then rise? Not God?
pass_b_english: The second catena form adds: “In Adam” stands for “because of Adam,” just as “in Christ” stands for “because of Christ.” So in Adam we die, clearly in the body, and in Christ they will be made alive, clearly in the body. If souls were alive before Christ, and after Christ it is again only souls that live, what did the saving plan add?

On 1 Corinthians 15:23–25: By “order” he means the order of the righteous and of the unrighteous. Here “those who are Christ's” does not mean the faithful in particular, but everyone, because all are Christ's. At his coming there will be the resurrection of all, when the end also comes: the drowning of death and of the devil, for this is the end of the world. By “the kingdom” he means not his own, but the one the evil one seized when he brought down Adam and those descended from him. In handing this kingdom over to the Father he will not be a stranger to it, for the Son reigns together with the Father. “Reign until” does not mark a time limit but emphasis, as if someone were to say, “I must live virtuously until I achieve righteousness.” He does not mean that once I have achieved it I will no longer live in righteousness, but that righteousness has to be achieved by me through virtuous effort. In the prophets too, “until” does not always mark a limit but emphasis, as in the Old Testament where he says, “I am, I am, until you grow old” (Isaiah 46:4). He does not say that the old age of those who grow old is the limit of his being, but that even when you grow old, I am: not growing old with you, but always being. So here too “until” marks the goal reached. What he means is this: his kingdom will not be broken off in the meantime, nor will believers fail, until what he purposed has been accomplished; and once he has accomplished it, he will reign without end.

On 1 Corinthians 15:29: If the bodies, he says, stay dead and do not rise, why are we baptized for these dead, as though they would rise and be judged, receiving forgiveness of sins so as not to be condemned?
On 1 Corinthians 15:32: As far as man could do it, he says, I fought with wild beasts, but God saved me.

On 1 Corinthians 15:35–38: The Greeks object that a seed once split no longer sprouts, and so neither is a man raised again if his foot has been cut off or his body maimed altogether. They do not know that the comparison is not of one nature with another, but with the power of the Maker. That is, who gave the seed its nature to sprout and its power as seed? Was it not God? Who makes the seed first die and then rise? Is it not God?

choices.why: Both spellings stand for the same contrast with προθεσμία; read ἐπίτασις in both.
πέρας as accomplishment fits the next sentence (he reigns until his purpose is achieved, then forever) without adding a negative.
Read as ἐπιλείψουσιν (itacism, same sound); 'seize' gives no sense. Noted.
